https://github.com/schildep/verified-3d-mesh-intersection

To my knowledge, this is the first formally verified implementation of a 3D constructive solid geometry (CSG) operation: mesh intersection, implemented in Lean 4 and verified against a concise specification that pins down the surface of the resulting mesh exactly and guarantees practical well-formedness conditions on the triangulation.

This project is also an experiment in avoiding having to trust AI-generated code. A human reviewer only needs to read 93 lines of formal specification and run the Lean checker to certify the correctness of the kernel, skipping the intricate 1000+ lines of AI-written implementation. To prove correctness, AI autonomously wrote over 60,000 lines of Lean proofs. I guided the agent through the milestones described in the readme to arrive at this result.

Also take a look at the web demo https://schildep.github.io/verified-3d-mesh-intersection/, which runs the verified mesh intersection kernel compiled from Lean to WebAssembly in your browser. Note that while the kernel is formally verified, the UI and glue code are not.

This is a really cool! The spec is nice, short and readable. This is how AI-generated code should be done!

Why do you define point as 

abbrev Point : Type := Fin 3 → Rat

and not as Vector Rat 3? Would that be the first major step in improving execution speed or it does not matter?

Also, there is not hope doing this for Float, right? As you can't even find intersection of two lines exactly. So it is unclear what the spec should say over Float.

I went back and forth on this: On Fin 3 -> Rat I automatically get a vector space structure, which I use in the spec. But on Vector Rat 3 I don’t, so the spec would be longer.

In the implementations there are optimizations equivalent to Vector Rat 3 and other optimizations like bounding volume hierarchies. In the interface, I intentionally kept it as simple as possible.

Regarding floats: We could use them internally:
Much of what the algorithm has to do is deciding geometrical predicates like on which side of a plane (defined by 3 points) another point is. Many performant CSG implementations have a separate layer that tries to use floats to decide inequalities like this and fall back to higher precision when floats are not sufficient. As I understand, this layer can be separated from the geometrical predicates we need, so we could formalize that arithmetic layer separately using axioms on floating point numbers and then plug it in the existing code. I think we could do that internally and still provide exact outputs and prove the same spec we have right now and the performance should increase a lot, since most of the computations right now is computing all these predicates exactly.

If you want floats in the interface and internally in all computations (not only to try to decide inequalities), I think it would would be more involved to think what the spec could look like to describe floating point errors in the output etc.

I see, yeah you could probably spoof the whole thing by providing trivial vector space structure on Vector Rat 3. So in the light of minimizing the spec the choice makes sense.

Regarding floats, very recently Lean has formal definition of Float now. You should update the project from v4.15.0! So it should be possible to use Float to do fast predicates in most cases.

Thank you for the tip! I didn’t know this was available. I now see it’s there in 4.33.0-rc1.

I already updated to v4.32.2 on a branch. I now pushed that branch update-to-v4.32.2 https://github.com/schildep/verified-3d-mesh-intersection/tree/update-to-v4.32.2 .

Did not merge the version update to main yet, because I think the webassembly build for the demo would get more complicated on newer lean versions.

I will try to use floats to improve performance.
how much tokens have been spent for the project?

I had a claude max 20x subscription while I was working on this project.
The main work was done over the duration of 2 weeks and I was hitting the limits of that subscription. It would have been much more expensive to pay for api costs than subscription.

As I describe in the readme I broke this up into milestones I described there.

I used Opus 4.8 for most of the work. While I was working on the project, Fable was available for a few days and I used it to plan implementation and write informal proofs before having Opus formalize it. That seemed to help. (Opus 4.8 by itself at least once got stuck in a loop trying to verify a helper function it had written, that had an obvious bug.)

Would be interesting to try out different models for this kind of implementation + verification work. e.g. OpenAI models and open weights models.

Amazing work! Saw you in hacker news and immediately inspired to learn Lean. Any thoughts on constraining the time/space complexity of the implementation?

Context: I'm exploring defining problems in Lean and let coding agents implement and prove. I tried a leetcode question (#22, generate all valid parenthesis sequence of length 2N) and its first attempt gave a trivial solution to enumerate the entire solution space (sequence of length 2N) and "filter" what satisfy my definition. The 2nd attempt I prompted it to "not enumerate all sequences" and it gave the standard backtracking solution with proof. However, that would defeat the purpose.

In my spec I left out time and memory requirements.

One can of course combine classical benchmarking based on concrete examples with a formal specification, and I think that can go a long way. But in principle, if you don‘t trust the agent that wrote the code, maybe it only optimized for the examples you benchmark.

It would be ideal to formally constrain everything we care about. (Maybe not only complexity but even give a bound with explicit constants.)

I am not sure, if there is a suitable framework for proving runtime constraints in Lean. I played around with „Isabelle-LLVM with time“ some time ago, and I was able to have an agent prove a runtime bound for a simpler geometrical problem. And there are other frameworks like this in other languages. In Lean there is CSLib that allows you to prove time complexity, but CSLib assumes that you truthfully annotate your implementation. I didn’t find anything in Lean that does not allow an agent to cheat by just not declaring the cost of an operation.

About the concrete problem of mesh intersection, there is another issue that you don‘t have in Leetcode problems: We would like the bound to be something like O(n log(n)) (at least in the number of bigint operations), but there are worst time configurations of inputs for which no algorithm can be better than O(n^2). (For example meshes where every triangle of one mesh intersects every triangle of the other mesh.) I have an idea what it would look like, but it would not be as simple as the rest of the specification to specify, which class of sequences of inputs, we actually care about when talking about runtime and to count actual operations in the computer rather than bigint operations.

Thanks!

I didn’t find anything in Lean that does not allow an agent to cheat by just not declaring the cost of an operation.

That's the initial thought I had as well (adding a cost to an operation) but it lands in the agent's territory.

Totally agree that for real-world problems like mesh operations it makes sense to assume some good properties about the input.
